newsitem.title: SPAIN: Economic rebound halts Bank of Spain rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: Economic rebound halts Bank of Spain rate cuts.

text.p: The Bank of Spain left its key money market rate unchanged on Thursday, as mounting evidence of a rebounding economy curbed the central bank's desire to continue cutting interest rates, analysts said.
A string of buoyant data in recent weeks suggests that the monetary easing cycle will be put on the back-burner until at least after the summer, analysts said.
"(Today's decision) was due to the combination of wage rises and a domestic consumption recovery," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
"Later in the year, the Bank of Spain will cut more, but they will have to do it in a more gradual way," he added.
The central bank has reduced its key interest rate 12 times since December 1995, slashing it from 9.25 percent to a current level of 5.25 percent. This year alone it has sanctioned four cuts.
Analysts said that while they did not expect rate reductions to continue at such a furious speed, they did not believe the market had seen the last of them.

Lumholdt said he expected the next rate cut at the end of August or the beginning of September, when the central bank could shave 25 basis points off its key rate. But that would leave it room to cut the rate by only another 25 bps by the end of the year, he added.

Analysts said the fact that recent falls in inflation had not spurred the central bank to cut rates this time was an indication that it would now be looking to other economic indicators to justify further rate cuts.
A decline in inflation to the lowest levels in nearly three decades has provided an incentive for many of the central bank's 12 cuts since 1995.
"The central bank will have to find ammunition in other areas of the economy than inflation after such strong rhetoric on wages and inflation," said an analyst at a Spanish bank in Madrid.

Last month, the Bank of Spain warned inflation would pick up during the rest of the year, but said it would remain below two percent in 1997 as a whole. The May CPI rose at a yearly rate of 1.5 percent, down from 1.7 percent in April.
Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato also warned at the end of June that wage rises which outstrip the inflation rate put new declines in interest rates in doubt.
Wages are rising at more than double the consumer price index rate, endangering medium-term inflation targets, and the government has admitted this is a worry.
First-quarter wages rose 4.2 percent a month on average, while the monthly inflation rate was 2.2 percent in March, 1.7 percent in April and 1.5 in May.
"The central bank has talked itself too hard into a corner," one analyst said.
Budget deficit data could provide the next focus for rate cuts, analysts said.

Bank of Spain governor Luis Angel Rojo painted a rosy picture of Spain's budgetary policy on Wednesday, saying the public deficit was set to fall sharply as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP).
As Spanish interest rates remain way above German rates, some analysts said the Bank of Spain had effectively voted for a more volatile currency rather than lower rates.

Given that the peseta is likely to enter European economic and monetary union (EMU) at a central parity of 85.07, the interest rate differential to Germany implies a stronger currency than at present, some analysts said.
"The peseta should be below 84.00 with such a wide differential and the central bank has therefore implicity voted for more volatility in the currency," one analyst said.

The Bank of Spain has kept a tight grip on the peseta in recent months, holding it in a range of 84.00 to 85.00 per mark in the run-up to EMU. On Thursday, the peseta was trading around 84.50 per mark.
